summary: For ages 5–7, teach the intuitive precursor to the water cycle: rain falls from clouds, and a drying puddle's water goes UP into the air (as invisible vapour we can't see), not out of existence. The core intellectual move is conservation — the water moved, it didn't vanish or only soak away — and that water can come back down as rain, a first up-and-down loop. Keep vocabulary everyday ('the sun warms the water and it goes into the air'); reserve 'evaporation/condensation/precipitation' for the later Water Cycle topic this feeds. Ground everything in first-hand, observable evidence before any diagram.
misconceptions: 'The puddle just disappeared / dried up into nothing.' — The water still exists; it moved into the air as invisible vapour (conservation).
'The water only soaked into the ground.' — Some may, but a puddle on tarmac also shrinks because water goes UP into the air; both can happen.
'Clouds are made of smoke/cotton wool.' — Clouds are tiny water droplets; at this age keep it to 'clouds are made of water' without over-detailing.
'Rain comes from the sky' with no link to clouds — make the cloud→rain connection explicit.
'The sun boils the puddle away' — evaporation happens at ordinary warmth, not boiling; avoid implying it must be hot enough to boil.

activities.title: The vanishing puddle: where did the water go?
steps: Watch (or drive) a fresh puddle after rain: mark where the puddle's edge starts, then let the sun warm it over time and watch the puddle shrink back from the marked line until it's gone.

In a pretend or animated scene, watch dots that stand for tiny bits of water rise from the puddle into the air. Explain that in real life we cannot see these bits, and that they spread out and only form clouds much higher up where the air is cold, not as a cloud right above the puddle.
Answer the prompt 'Where did the water go?' out loud before any explanation is given.

In the pretend scene, make it rain from the cloud and watch water come back down to refill the puddle. Explain that in real life rain falls in lots of places, so the same water does not land back in the same puddle.
Say in the child's own words where the water went and whether it was lost.
activities.insight: The puddle's water did not disappear or cease to exist — it went up into the air (as invisible vapour) and can come back down again as rain. Water moves up and down; it is conserved.

activities.title: First-hand drying investigation (saucer in the sun)
steps: Put the same shallow amount of water in two saucers, cover one with cling film and leave the other uncovered, and leave both in a warm or sunny spot.
Before observing, predict what will happen to the water and say WHY (many predict it will simply dry up and be gone) — state the reason out loud.
Return later to look at the underside of the film and describe the droplets that have collected there.

Discuss: the water in the open saucer went down or disappeared, but under the film it stayed in and droplets formed on the film. Where did those droplets come from, and where did the open saucer's water go?
activities.insight: Water that leaves the saucer isn't destroyed — it rises as invisible vapour and can be caught again as droplets on a cover, showing it still exists.

activities.title: Invisible water you can show
steps: Breathe on a cold window or mirror and watch it fog, then describe where the mist came from.
Connect to everyday experiences: wet washing drying, wet hair drying, and the misty 'steam' over a hot bath (tiny drops of water we can see, made when invisible water in the air cools).
Explain why we usually can't see the water that goes into the air, even though it is still there.
activities.insight: Water can be in the air as invisible vapour; we can make it visible again on a cold surface, which makes 'unseen water' believable and non-magical.

activities.title: Puddle detective: explain it yourself
steps: Respond to a curious prompt — 'There was a puddle here this morning, and nobody tipped it out or mopped it up. Where did it go, and is it gone forever?'
Give a full explanation in the child's own words.

Answer probe questions: 'If the water went into the air, why can't we see it?', 'Could that same water come back down to the ground? How?', 'What if we covered the puddle with a clear lid — where would the water go then?'
activities.insight: The child can articulate the conservation idea and the up-and-back-down loop unprompted, distinguishing 'moved into the air' from 'gone'.

checkQuestion: There was a puddle in the playground yesterday, and today it's gone — but nobody tipped it out or mopped it up. Where did the water go, and is it gone forever?
checkAnswer: The water went up into the air as invisible water vapour — it evaporated. It isn't gone or destroyed, it's just spread out in the air where we can't see it. Later that same water can form clouds and fall back down as rain.
